title: Coil vs Air UV Lights: What's the Difference?
h1: Coil Sterilization vs Air Sterilization UV Lights: What's the Difference?
description: Coil UV lights keep the AC coil and drain pan free of mold and slime. Air UV lights treat moving air. Learn how they differ and which one fits your home.
quick_answer: A coil UV light shines continuously on the AC coil and drain pan to stop mold and bacteria from growing on those wet surfaces. An air UV light is placed in the ductwork to treat microbes in the air as it passes by. Coil lights are the more common choice for homes. Air lights need stronger output and careful placement to do much.
body:
What does a coil UV light do?

Your indoor AC coil gets cold and wet every time the system cools, and the drain pan under it holds water. In a dark cabinet, that's ideal for biofilm, the slimy layer of mold and bacteria that builds up on coil fins and in pans and drain lines.

A coil light is a UV-C lamp mounted near the coil, usually in the coil cabinet or supply plenum, aimed at the coil face and pan. It typically runs 24 hours a day. Because the coil and pan sit still under the light, they get a steady dose that keeps growth from taking hold.

What you get:

  • A cleaner coil that holds its airflow and efficiency longer
  • Less slime in the drain pan and condensate line, so fewer clogs
  • Fewer musty smells when the system starts

What does an air UV light do?

An air sterilization light is installed in the return or supply duct with the goal of treating microbes in the air as they flow past. Since air moves through the duct quickly, each particle only spends a moment in the light. To make that moment count, air systems use higher-output lamps, often several of them, placed along a straight run of duct.

Some air systems are wired to run only when the blower runs. Others run continuously. Either way, they reduce live microbes in the airstream but don't sterilize the air in a single pass, and they don't remove dust, pollen or dander at all.

How do coil and air UV lights compare?

Coil UV lightAir UV light
Main targetCoil, drain pan, nearby surfacesMicrobes in moving air
Where it goesCoil cabinet or plenum near the coilReturn or supply duct
Typical run timeAround the clockWith the blower, or continuously
Lamp outputLowerHigher, sometimes multiple lamps
Best forCoil slime, drain clogs, musty smellsHouseholds focused on airborne germs
Doesn't doRemove dust or allergensRemove dust or allergens

Which UV light is right for my home?

For most homes, a coil light is the practical choice. It solves a real, visible problem, and it's especially useful in coastal San Diego and Orange County homes where marine air keeps the air handler damp. If you have recurring drain line clogs or a musty startup smell, start here.

An air light can make sense for households that are especially concerned about airborne germs, such as when someone in the home has a weakened immune system. Even then, it works best alongside a good filter, and sometimes a portable HEPA purifier in key rooms.

Some systems combine both functions in one unit. If you go that route, make sure the lamp placement actually covers the coil and has enough air exposure to matter.

Do UV lights replace coil cleaning?

Not entirely. A coil lamp keeps biological growth down, but dust that slips past the filter still lands on the coil, and UV does nothing to that. You'll still want the coil inspected during regular maintenance. What usually changes is how often it needs a full cleaning, since the sticky biofilm that traps dust is kept under control.

What should you know before installing either type?

  • Choose ozone-free lamps. Ozone irritates the lungs.
  • Protect nearby plastics. UV-C slowly breaks down flex duct liners, plastic pans and wire insulation it shines on. Good placement and shielding prevent that.
  • Plan for bulb replacement. UV-C output fades before the bulb looks dim. Follow the manufacturer's replacement interval.
  • Use a safety switch. The lamp should shut off when the cabinet is opened. Never look at a lit UV-C bulb.
  • Clean the coil first if it's already dirty. UV keeps a coil clean, but it's slow at clearing heavy buildup.

Not sure which fits your system? Our indoor air quality technicians can look at your air handler and ducts and recommend the right setup, or tell you if better filtration would help more.
faqs: Can one UV light do both coil and air sterilization?

Some units are marketed for both. A lamp placed near the coil will treat the coil well and give passing air a brief dose. For meaningful air treatment you generally need more output and exposure time, which is why dedicated air systems use stronger lamps.
Do coil UV lights help with allergies?

Indirectly. They keep mold from growing on the coil and in the drain pan, so the system isn't adding spores and musty odors to the air. They don't capture pollen, dust or dander. For those, you need a good filter.
Should a UV light run all the time?

Coil lights are designed to run continuously, since the coil and pan stay damp even when the system is off. Air lights are sometimes wired to run only with the blower, since there's no air moving to treat otherwise.
How long do HVAC UV bulbs last?
Bulbs keep glowing long after their germicidal output has dropped, so they're replaced on a schedule. Follow the lamp manufacturer's interval, which is often about once a year.
